She kept her gestures to a minimum and her tone was consistently soft throughout the entire performance. Despite her grammatical errors, she still effectively narrates the general plot. In this instance, her delivery made more of an impact than the story itself.

all_comparisons.label: collection_context
all_comparisons.reference_text: My mom learned of this story from her mother when she was a child in Saigon, Vietnam in the late 1950s or early 1960s. Her mother told her many stories when she was a kid. As a language teacher in Vietnam, my mom also passed these stories on to her younger students. This one was very popular story among the kids. It parallels the American version called Cinderella. She remembers mainly adults transmitting folktales to younger children. Older kids no longer had an interest in fairytales and found no use for them in conversations with their friends.

all_comparisons.label: collector_annotation
all_comparisons.reference_text: This is one of the most told stories from Vietnamese tradition. It unsurprisingly conforms to the feminist notion that women are portrayed in a negative light. The virtuous female character has no agency. She does what her stepmother tells her to without objection. Her contribution to the household involves cleaning, cooking, and everything related to the woman’s realm. In the absence of a father figure, her stepmother takes on the male role and confines her to the kitchen. Tam helplessly surrenders every time a problem arises. She resorts to relying on the Goddess for assistance.

all_comparisons.reference_text: “This is a story about a cowherd and a weaver girl. Originally, the two did not know each other, and were very efficient workers. The boy herded cows well, and the girl wove nice cloth; both did very good work. One day, they met, and fell in love. Soon, they were always playing together and neglecting their work. This made the gods very angry because they forgot about their responsibilities. The gods decided to punish them and cast them away to opposite sides of the Milky Way. Although the gods were angry, they pitied the young lovers and allowed them to meet once a year. When the sparrows lined up along the sky to form a bridge, on July 7 of every [lunar calendar] year, the lovers would be able to meet. This day is called “chi shi ( in Chinese; it means “night of seven.” And this is the origin of Chinese Valentine’s Day, which is on July 7th of the lunar calendar.”

all_comparisons.reference_text: Another thing to consider is the traditional ideals of beauty in Asian societies. Many women during that time believed that attractiveness equates small feet and white skin, because this particular definition of beauty correlates to a high social status. Women from wealthier backgrounds usually enjoyed a less demanding way of life. They did not have to overexert themselves like the working-class. Women from underprivileged families had to endure rough working conditions in the fields, resulting in their darkened pigmentation and larger hands and feet. Filial duties also played an important part in Vietnamese society. Confucius principles greatly affected how children interacted with their parents. Respect for elders and parents came before anything else.

This proverb, which is used by both male and female adults, is most often directed towards young people in their late teens and early twenties.
